title: DOJ Warns Democratic Senator of ‘Legal Consequences’ Over Trump Investigations—What Can It Actually Do?
author: Tiago Ventura
body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) has warned Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts that she could face "significant legal consequences" if she fails to preserve records related to potential Congressional investigations involving allies of President Donald Trump.

The warning came in a letter from Aaron Reitz, the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas, who accused Warren, the likely incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, of appearing "eager to wield your future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of President Trump's private associates."

The letter, shared by Reitz on social media Sunday and later reposted by Trump on Truth Social, is the latest warning directed at Congressional Democrats over their plans to launch a blitz of investigations into the Trump Administration and its allies, after the party’s sweeping midterm victories gave the party control of the House and Senate.

“Democrats cannot use their Congressional investigations powers to punish Americans for exercising their First Amendment rights,” a White House official tells TIME.

Reitz called on Warren to preserve materials related to potential investigations involving Trump's allies, accusing her of seeking to target private individuals associated with the President.

“I am writing to give you formal notice of your obligation to preserve all documents, communications, and other electronically stored information relevant to your intent to weaponize congressional investigations,” he wrote.

Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, has long been a vocal critic of Wall Street and of the Trump Administration's policies.

Reitz's letter cited Warren's Nov. 8 interview on CBS News's Face the Nation, in which she discussed investigating corporate leaders who may have broken the law. Reitz argued that her remarks "sends a strong smoke signal" that she intends to target individuals close to Trump.

He also pointed to an op-ed Warren wrote for TIME, after the Democrats' midterm results, in which the Senator argued that delivering accountability was one of the reasons behind the party's sweeping midterm victories.

“Congress has the power to hold Donald Trump and his cronies accountable for ripping off the American people to make themselves richer. Big Tech CEOs, Wall Street executives, and giant corporations should prepare to answer tough questions and face meaningful consequences if they have broken the law,” she wrote.

TIME has reached out to Warren's office for comment.

What could the DOJ do?

Legal experts tell TIME that Congress has broad powers to investigate the executive branch and other matters connected to its legislative responsibilities, authority granted implicitly by the Constitution.

“It's not explicit in the Constitution, but it's inherent in the legislative branch, and that's what the Supreme Court has stated numerous times,” Dave Rapallo, an associate professor of law at Georgetown Law, tells TIME. “Congress has a constitutional power to conduct investigations for valid legislative branch purposes, and those could be to inform legislation prior to making appropriations, to monitor how taxpayer funds are being spent, to root out waste, fraud, [or] abuse.”

Rapallo explains that these powers can also extend to potential wrongdoing involving private individuals and businesses, provided the investigations serve a legitimate legislative purpose.

“Congress's investigative power is very, very broad. For example, if donors are contributing millions of dollars to the upgrade of a U.S. facility like the White House, Congress has the right and authority to oversee those donations,” he says. “If there are allegations that there is some sort of pay-to-play scheme or other type of abuse, Congress has authority to run down those allegations.”

Experts explain that the warning sent to Warren is a document preservation letter, a notice requesting that potentially relevant records and communications be retained. Such letters can precede legal proceedings or investigations, but the notice itself does not amount to a criminal charge or a court order halting Congressional oversight.

“They're not unusual if a criminal investigation has been authorized, whether it's by the Justice Department or another law enforcement agency,” says Rapallo, adding that normally such a request might be followed by a subpoena. In Warren's case, however, “there has been no explanation of any criminal wrongdoing, and so it's unclear what the basis is to send a document preservation letter.”

Although Reitz cited federal criminal civil-rights statutes in his letter, alleging that congressional investigations could be used to violate the rights of people associated with Trump, he did not identify specific criminal conduct by Warren or announce any charges against her.

Jenny Carroll, a professor of law at Texas A&M University, says the letter appears to be more of a warning about a potential investigation than evidence of an established criminal case. She describes the DOJ as “investigating that possibility, and asking to preserve any of the evidence that would allow [them] to make a determination of whether or not [Warren] violated the laws of the United States.”

While Reitz invokes federal criminal civil-rights statutes, Carroll argues that “none of that is stated with any specificity.”

“What are the elements of these U.S. code sections that you actually think are violated? What facts support your claim that this violation has occurred, and what exactly are the sanctions or the penalties? There's no criminal charge against the Senator at this point,” she says.

Rapallo similarly says that although the DOJ appears to “suggest that there could be criminal exposure,” the letter does not make clear what conduct would constitute a crime.

Experts also point to the Constitutional protections available to lawmakers conducting legitimate Congressional investigations.

The Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause protects members of Congress from being questioned "in any other place" for legislative acts undertaken as part of their official duties.

“The letter blurs two separate questions: whether a congressional investigative act serves a valid legislative purpose, which courts resolve if and when a recipient refuses to comply, and that, at most, ends with the subpoena going unenforced, and whether the inquiry itself constitutes a crime,” Molly Nixon, a senior fellow in Executive Power at the Cato Institute, tells TIME.

“The criminal statutes the letter cites require proving a specific intent to deprive someone of a federal right, but the Constitution’s Speech or Debate clause bars prosecutors from probing the motivations underlying a legislative act," she says. "Accordingly, Reitz’s letter is on shaky legal footing.”

Against that legal backdrop, some experts argue that the warning may be intended to discourage Warren from pursuing investigations once Democrats regain control of Congress.

“It does feel like it's an effort to chill or to discourage her activity,” says Carroll, adding that Warren has so far largely discussed her plans publicly rather than taken actions that would constitute grounds for a criminal investigation.

Carroll says there isn't “any activity that would really warrant any sort of investigation, so it feels like it's designed to make her stop.”

Other Democrats face similar DOJ warnings

Warren is not the only congressional Democrat to face warnings from the Trump Administration over plans to investigate the President and his allies.

Last week, Trump ordered the DOJ to look into Democratic lawmakers whom he accused of "threatening" people, while Attorney General Todd Blanche subsequently indicated that his department was prepared to challenge congressional Democrats over their use of oversight powers.

“What we are going to do to defend the Administration, defend President Trump, and defend anybody who works in the Executive is make sure that Congress stays within their very specific, very narrow world that they're allowed to operate, which is to do oversight,” Blanche said in an interview with Fox News on Sunday.

Reitz has also issued similar warnings to other Democratic lawmakers who are preparing to take on influential Congressional oversight roles.

In his Sunday letter to Warren, Reitz cited a Nov. 11 letter signed by Warren, Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, and Representative Robert Garcia of California. The lawmakers had asked Meredith O'Rourke, a National Park Foundation board member and top fundraiser for Trump, to retain documents related to funding for the White House ballroom and other projects.

Reitz accused the three lawmakers of “demanding sweeping information about her and other private citizens and entities who associate with President Trump.”

The warning comes as these Democrats prepare to take control of congressional committees in January. Garcia is expected to lead the House Oversight Committee, while Blumenthal is set to chair the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee's Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

Blumenthal had already received a similar letter from Reitz on Nov. 11, warning of "significant legal consequences” if records related to his oversight investigations were not preserved.

In a letter sent to Reitz the same day, Blumenthal defended his right to investigate the circumstances under which corporations donated millions of dollars to projects supported by Trump. He also directed Reitz to preserve records and correspondence with the White House and senior Justice Department officials related to the warning.

"I will not be intimidated," Blumenthal wrote.

Rapallo argues that the response from the DOJ is particularly notable because Republican lawmakers have made similar promises to investigate Democratic administrations in the past without facing comparable warnings.

“Republican members of Congress have made very similar comments about exercising their oversight and investigative powers, and have never received this sort of reception from the Justice Department,” he says, describing the warnings as an “approach to try to push Democratic members back on their heels, based on a pretty flimsy basis.”

Reitz also sent a letter on Nov. 12 to Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, citing comments she made in an interview with CNN's Jake Tapper where she faced questions about remarks made on Vox's podcast America, Actually, where she spoke about holding people associated with Trump accountable once Democrats regained control of the Senate.

Slotkin denounced the move during a Nov. 13 press conference as a “tell-tale sign of an authoritarian," accusing the President of “trying to criminally indict people for the words they say against him.”
